Yes, the court properly admitted the child’s identification statement and affirmed the conviction.

4 Quick Rule Key takeaway

A child’s out-of-court identification is admissible if the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination.

Clarifies that testimonial out-of-court identifications by child victims are admissible if the child testifies and can be cross-examined, affecting hearsay doctrine and confrontation practice.

Out-of-court statements made by a child abuse victim identifying their abuser may be admitted if the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination, reducing concerns typically associated with hearsay.

# Nathaniel Patrick Azure was convicted of three counts of assault with a dangerous weapon and three counts of discharging or…

A man living on the Spirit Lake Reservation in North Dakota was accused of committing several violent crimes over the course of about a year and a half.
...
## What happened
...
The charges said he shot one person in January 2021, pulled a gun on another person in May 2022, and shot a third person the very next day. All three incidents happened on the reservation. He was charged with six crimes in total — three counts of assault with a dangerous weapon and three counts of using a firearm during a violent crime.

Before the trial began, the government told the defendant it planned to use records from his Facebook account as evidence. The defendant objected. He argued that the paperwork certifying those records was not good enough because it gave no way to contact the person at Meta who signed it. He said he could not verify whether that person was real or actually worked there. The trial court disagreed and allowed the records in, pointing out that the law sets a low bar for proving evidence is genuine, and that other witnesses could also connect him to the account.

During the trial, a federal agent testified about the investigation. At one point, the prosecutor asked the agent whether the defendant had agreed to give a DNA sample by mouth swab. The agent said the defendant had refused. The defendant's lawyer did not object at the time. The next morning, the defendant's legal team asked the judge to declare a mistrial, saying the question was improper because it drew attention to the defendant exercising his legal right to say no. The judge refused to end the trial but did give the jury a special instruction, telling them they could not treat the refusal as a sign of guilt. The judge repeated that instruction at the end of the trial.

The jury found the defendant guilty on all counts.

The federal judicial system is organized into three tiers, with the U.S. Circuit Courts of Appeals serving a crucial intermediate role. These courts function as the primary appellate level for federal cases, standing just below the Supreme Court of the United States. The Circuit Courts were established to manage the vast number of appeals geographically, reviewing decisions that originate from the lower federal trial courts, known as District Courts. The entire nation is divided into twelve regional circuits and one federal circuit, each responsible for appeals arising within its specific geographic boundaries. The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals is one of these regional divisions, overseeing a significant area of the American Midwest.

## Defining the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals

The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals operates as an intermediate appellate body, reviewing the final judgments and orders of the U.S. District Courts located within its jurisdiction. It analyzes the record from the trial court to determine if a legal error occurred that warrants reversing or modifying the lower court’s decision. The Circuit Courts were geographically organized by Congress to facilitate the efficient handling of the federal appellate caseload. The decisions of the Eighth Circuit are final unless the Supreme Court grants a petition for a writ of certiorari. The court currently has eleven authorized judicial posts for its active judges, who typically hear cases in panels of three.

## The States Comprising the Eighth Circuit

The geographic jurisdiction of the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals encompasses seven states located in the Midwest region: Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota. webiq.title: United States v. Nathaniel Azure | Docket Audit
webiq.snippet:
Before the trial began, the government told the defendant it planned to use records from his Facebook account as evidence. The defendant objected. He argued that the paperwork certifying those records was not good enough because it gave no way to contact the person at Meta who signed it. He said he could not verify whether that person was real or actually worked there. The trial court disagreed and allowed the records in, pointing out that the law sets a low bar for proving evidence is genuine, and that other witnesses could also connect him to the account.

During the trial, a federal agent testified about the investigation. At one point, the prosecutor asked the agent whether the defendant had agreed to give a DNA sample by mouth swab. The agent said the defendant had refused. The defendant's lawyer did not object at the time. The next morning, the defendant's legal team asked the judge to declare a mistrial, saying the question was improper because it drew attention to the defendant exercising his legal right to say no. The judge refused to end the trial but did give the jury a special instruction, telling them they could not treat the refusal as a sign of guilt. The judge repeated that instruction at the end of the trial.

The jury found the defendant guilty on all counts. The judge sentenced him to 384 months — 32 years — in prison. 

The appeals court upheld the conviction and agreed with every decision the trial court made. On the DNA question, the court said that even if the prosecutor's question was improper, it was too brief and too small a moment in a long trial to have unfairly hurt the defendant. The government had also presented strong independent evidence of guilt — including eyewitness testimony from the victims themselves and from bystanders — and the judge's curative instruction told the jury not to hold the refusal against the defendant.

Taken together, that was enough evidence for the jury to decide whether the records were authentic.
